claims.claim: A single wild-type allele of TIR1 or AFB2 is sufficient to support growth throughout development.
claims.source: and yet a single wild-type allele of TIR1 or AFB2 is sufficient to support growth throughout development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the viability of tir1/+ afb12345 and afb2/+ tir1afb1345 plants shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: There is extensive functional overlap between even the most distantly related TIR1/AFB genes except for AFB1.
claims.source: Our analysis reveals extensive functional overlap between even the most distantly related TIR1/AFB genes except for AFB1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the genetic analysis of all 63 mutant combinations.

claims.claim: AFB1 has a specialized function in rapid auxin-dependent inhibition of root growth and early phase of root gravitropism.
claims.source: Surprisingly, AFB1 has a specialized function in rapid auxin-dependent inhibition of root growth and early phase of root gravitropism.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: AFB1's specialized activity may be related to a difference in subcellular localization compared to the other members of the family.
claims.source: This activity may be related to a difference in subcellular localization compared to the other members of the family.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by fluorescence quantification data in Figure 5S showing AFB1-mCitrine is primarily cytoplasmic.

claims.claim: Three clades of auxin receptors were established prior to the radiation of euphyllophytes (ferns plus seed plants) over 400 million years ago.
claims.source: While the last common ancestors of land plants and of vascular plants had only one TIR1/AFB gene, three clades of auxin receptors were established prior to the radiation of euphyllophytes (ferns plus seed plants) over 400 million years ago (Morris et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, with citation to Morris et al., 2018.

claims.claim: AFB6 orthologs are not present in the genomes of core Brassicales species including Arabidopsis, nor those of Poaceae species including rice and maize.
claims.source: For example, AFB6 orthologs are not present in the genomes of core Brassicales species—including Arabidopsis—nor those of Poaceae species including rice and maize.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The gene duplication event establishing the distinct TIR1 and AFB1 clades is coincident with the At-β WGD event at the base of Brassicales.
claims.source: The gene duplication event establishing the distinct TIR1 and AFB1 clades is coincident with the At-β WGD event at the base of Brassicales, while both the AFB2/AFB3 and the AFB4/AFB5 duplication events coincide with the more recent At-α WGD prior to divergence of the Brassicaceae family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Schranz and Mitchell-Olds, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Schranz and Mitchell-Olds, 2006.

claims.claim: Since the last common ancestor of Arabidopsis and Tarenaya, the AFB1 gene has accumulated over three times as many non-synonymous changes as TIR1.
claims.source: Since the last common ancestor of Arabidopsis (Brassicaceae) and Tarenaya (Cleomaceae), the AFB1 gene has accumulated over three times as many non-synonymous changes as TIR1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by branch length data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: AFB1 is under selection based on the ratio of non-synonymous and synonymous substitutions.
claims.source: despite being under selection based on the ratio of non-synonymous and synonymous substitutions (Delker et al., 2010; Wright et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Delker et al., 2010 and Wright et al., 2017.

claims.claim: AFB1 contains two of three substitutions in the first α-helix of the F-Box that were each previously shown to weaken TIR1's interaction with CUL1.
claims.source: AFB1 also differs from the other TIR1/AFBs in that it contains two of three substitutions in the first α-helix of the F-Box that were each previously shown to weaken TIR1's interaction with CUL1 (Yu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Yu et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The Glu8Lys substitution in AFB1 appeared shortly after the At-β WGD that produced AFB1.
claims.source: The substitution with the largest effect, Glu8Lys (equivalent to Glu12Lys in TIR1), appeared shortly after the At-β WGD that produced AFB1, and the Phe14Leu substitution appeared prior to the crown group of the Brassicaceae family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phylogenetic data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The tir1-1 allele does not act as a dominant-negative allele.
claims.source: However, we found that the root elongation phenotype of plants heterozygous for the tir1-1, tir1-10, and tir1-9 alleles were not significantly different from each other and each displays a semi-dominant phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B). These results argue against a dominant negative effect for tir1-1 since neither tir1-9 or tir1-10 produce detectable levels of transcript (Ruegger et al., 1998; Parry et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, with citations to Ruegger et al., 1998 and Parry et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The sixty-three mutant combinations displayed a wide range of phenotypes from indistinguishable from wild type to early-embryo lethality.
claims.source: The sixty-three mutant combinations displayed a wide range of phenotypes from indistinguishable from wild type to early-embryo lethality (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The three viable quintuple mutants—tir1afb1245, tir1afb1345, and afb12345—had rosettes approximately half the diameter and inflorescences less than half the height of WT Col-0.
claims.source: The three viable quintuple mutants—tir1afb1245, tir1afb1345, and afb12345—had rosettes approximately half the diameter and inflorescences less than half the height of WT Col-0.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by measurements in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Lines retaining only one copy of TIR1 (tir1/+ afb12345) or one copy of AFB2 (afb2/+ tir1afb1345) were viable.
claims.source: Remarkably, lines retaining only one copy of TIR1 (tir1/+ afb12345) or one copy of AFB2 (afb2/+ tir1afb1345) were viable.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The afb2/+ tir1afb1345 and tir1/+ afb12345 plants rarely produced seeds.
claims.source: The afb2/+ tir1afb1345 and tir1/+ afb12345 plants rarely produced seeds.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observation of the plants.

claims.claim: 32% of tir1afb1245 siliques have only one valve.
claims.source: Normal siliques (Col-0, left) have two valves containing developing seeds while 32% of tir1afb1245 siliques have only one.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1C caption and shown in the image.

claims.claim: The tir1 mutation had the largest effect on root elongation inhibition by auxin.
claims.source: For both the root elongation assay and the induction of lateral root primordia, the tir1 allele had the largest effect with the afb2, afb5, afb3, and afb4 mutations having smaller median effects (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The afb1 mutation had little or no effect on root elongation.
claims.source: The afb1 mutation had little or no effect on root elongation but, surprisingly, had an opposite effect on lateral root formation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The afb1 mutation had an opposite effect on lateral root formation compared to other TIR1/AFB mutations.
claims.source: The afb1 mutation had little or no effect on root elongation but, surprisingly, had an opposite effect on lateral root formation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The afb1 mutation suppressed the lateral root phenotype of the afb234 triple mutant.
claims.source: We found that the afb1 mutation suppressed the phenotype of both the afb234 (2.15 ± 0.13 versus 1.75 ± 0.10 lateral roots/cm) and afb345 triple mutants (3.10 ± 0.13 versus 1.96 ± 0.14 lateral roots/cm) measured after 12 days on media not supplemented with IAA.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific measurements provided.

claims.claim: The afb2345 quadruple mutant is over 6 cm smaller in rosette diameter than each of the four triple mutants.
claims.source: However, they have huge collective effects, where the afb2345 quadruple mutant is over 6 cm smaller than each of the four triple mutants (blue arrowheads; Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and indicated in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The afb5 mutation has the largest effect on inflorescence branching and height.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports that AFB5 plays a key role in regulating inflorescence branching and height (Prigge et al., 2016; Ligerot et al., 2017), the afb5 mutation has the largest effect on these phenotypes, although each mutation, except for afb1, had some effect (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Prigge et al., 2016 and Ligerot et al., 2017, and shown in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: The penetrance of the rootless seedling phenotype for tir1afb23, tir1afb123, and tir1afb245 lines was significantly lower at 20°C than at either 17°C or 23°C.
claims.source: The penetrance of the phenotype for all three lines was significantly lower at 20°C than at either 17°C or 23°C for all with the exception that the difference with tir1afb245 at 17°C was not significant using the Fisher's exact test.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claims.claim: Aspects of the auxin regulatory system are sensitive to temperature.
claims.source: This suggests that aspects of the auxin regulatory system are sensitive to temperature.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the temperature-dependent penetrance data.

claims.claim: Approximately one-quarter of embryos from tir1/+ afb235 or afb2/+ tir1afb35 plants lacked cotyledons and had over-proliferated suspensors.
claims.source: Eleven of 41 (27%) and 52 of 213 (24%), respectively, of the embryos from each line lacked cotyledons and had over-proliferated suspensors while the rest had a WT phenotype (Figure 3A, A').
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 3A, A'.

claims.claim: The initial division of the embryo proper was occasionally displaced from vertical in sextuple mutant 2-cell embryos compared to complemented siblings.
claims.source: The earliest potential difference between sextuple mutants and the complemented siblings is that the initial division of the embryo proper was occasionally displaced from vertical in sextuple 2-cell embryos (3 of 19 were >12° from vertical) compared to complemented sibling embryos (0 of 64), however the average angles from vertical were not significantly different (p=0.32) (Figure 3B–C versus 3B′–C′, 3N).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 3B-C, B'-C', and 3N.

claims.claim: The curvature of the lower surface of the upper tier in 8-cell embryos is significantly more prominent in sextuple mutants than in complemented siblings.
claims.source: The third round of divisions in the embryo proper separates the upper and lower tiers with the lower surface of the upper tier typically being slightly convex, and this curvature is significantly more prominent in the sextuple mutants (p=1.4 × 10−7; Figure 3D versus 3D′, 3O).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical significance and shown in Figure 3D, D', and 3O.

claims.claim: 69% of cell divisions during the transition from 8-cell to 16-cell embryos are anticlinal in sextuple mutant embryos, compared to nearly all being periclinal in complemented embryos.
claims.source: Later, during the transition from the 8-cell to the 16-cell embryos, nearly all cell divisions in the complemented embryos are oriented periclinally, as in WT embryos. In contrast, 69% of these division are anticlinal in the mutant embryos (Figure 3E and E', 3P).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3E, E', and 3P.

claims.claim: The asymmetric division of the hypophysis cell was delayed in sextuple mutant embryos and when it occurred, was symmetrical.
claims.source: In WT 32-cell stage embryos, the hypophysis cell normally divides asymmetrically to produce the lens-shaped cell which is required for the formation of the embryonic root. This division was delayed in the mutant, and when it occurred, was symmetrical (Figure 3G–H and 3G′–H′).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3G-H and G'-H'.

claims.claim: Cells of the sextuple mutant embryo proper slow or cease dividing and the cells of the suspensor begin to proliferate.
claims.source: Later, the cells of the embryo proper slow or cease dividing and the cells of the suspensor begin to proliferate and invariably produce a radially symmetric terminal phenotype (Figure 3I–M, 3I′–M′).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3I-M and I'-M'.

claims.claim: Around the bent-cotyledon stage, the cells of the sextuple mutant senesce and seed development is aborted.
claims.source: Around the stage where complemented siblings are at the bent-cotyledon stage, the cells of the sextuple mutant senesce and seed development is aborted (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The sextuple mutant reveals the importance of TIR1/AFB auxin response machinery from the earliest stages of embryogenesis.
claims.source: Hence, the sextuple mutant reveals the importance of TIR1/AFB auxin response machinery from the earliest stages of embryogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the embryo phenotype data.

claims.claim: Expression of the auxin-responsive marker DR5rev:3×Venus-N7 was undetectable in tir1afb235 quadruple mutant embryos.
claims.source: Expression of the auxin-responsive marker DR5rev:3×Venus-N7 was undetectable in embryos displaying the mutant phenotype (Figure 4E–G; compare to Figure 4A–C; 0/10 in quadruple mutants and 26/26 in non-mutant siblings) indicating that auxin-regulated transcription through the remaining receptors, AFB4 and AFB1, is minimal at most during embryogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4E-G compared to 4A-C.

claims.claim: The quiescent center marker WOX5:GFP was not detected in tir1afb235 mutant embryos.
claims.source: Similarly, the quiescent center marker WOX5:GFP was not detected in the mutant embryos (Figure 4H), whereas in wild type the reporter is first expressed in the hypophysis prior to its asymmetric division then persists in the quiescent center cells (Figure 4D; 0/11 in quadruple mutants and 28/28 in non-mutant siblings).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4H compared to 4D.

claims.claim: PIN7-Venus signal is much stronger in protodermal cells of the embryo proper in tir1afb235 mutant embryos compared to wild type.
claims.source: In mutant embryos, PIN7-Venus is faintly detectable in these cells in globular-stage embryos. Unexpectedly, the signal is much stronger in protodermal cells of the embryo proper, especially in the lower tier, by the 32-cell stage (Figure 4O–P; 7/8 quadruple mutants and 0/14 siblings).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4O-P.

claims.claim: PIN1-Venus signal is reduced and restricted primarily to apical protodermal cells in tir1afb235 mutant embryos.
claims.source: In the mutants, PIN1-Venus signal is reduced and restricted primarily to apical protodermal cells (Figure 4M–N; 9/9 quadruple mutants).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4M-N.

claims.claim: NTT-YPet is progressively lost in the distal suspensor cells before abnormal lateral cell divisions occur in tir1afb235 mutant embryos.
claims.source: In mutants, NTT-YPet appears normally in most suspensor cells, but not always including the hypophysis (2/6 32-cell quadruple mutant embryos had signal above background in the hypophysis), and is progressively lost in the distal suspensor cells before the abnormal lateral cell divisions occur (Figure 4V–X; 4/4 late-globular-stage mutants lacked signal in both the hypophysis and the adjacent suspensor cell).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4V-X.

claims.claim: Gametophytically-expressed TIR1/AFBs do not contribute to gametophytic viability.
claims.source: This indicates that gametophytically expressed TIR1/AFBs do not contribute to gametophytic viability.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on transmission rate data in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: The sextuple mutant was transmitted nearly as well without the complementing transgene as with it through both the pollen (49.4%) and the female gametophyte (47.9%).
claims.source: The sextuple mutant was transmitted nearly as well as without the complementing transgene as with it through both the pollen (49.4%) and the female gametophyte (47.9%) (χ2 test p=0.81 and 0.43, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific percentages and statistical tests.

claims.claim: AFB5-mCitrine fluorescent signal was fairly uniformly distributed in shoot apices.
claims.source: The fluorescent signal in the AFB5-mCitrine lines was fairly uniformly distributed in shoot apices (Figure 5F)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: In AFB3-mCitrine, AFB2-mCitrine, and TIR1-mCitrine lines, fluorescence was more restricted to young primordia and meristem peripheral zones.
claims.source: while in the AFB3-mCitrine, AFB2-mCitrine, and TIR1-mCitrine lines, fluorescence was more restricted to young primordia and meristem peripheral zones (Figure 5A and C–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A, C-D.

claims.claim: TIR1-mCitrine appears to be strongest in the adaxial domains of the youngest primordia.
claims.source: Within organ primordia, TIR1-mCitrine appears to be strongest in the adaxial domains of the youngest primordia.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observation of fluorescence patterns.

claims.claim: Signal for the AFB4-mCitrine line was barely detectable.
claims.source: Signal for the AFB4-mCitrine line was barely detectable (Figure 5E)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: AFB1-mCitrine signal was very strong and largely complementary to TIR1-mCitrine, with the strongest signal in abaxial domains and in the stem.
claims.source: while that of AFB1-mCitrine was very strong and largely complementary to TIR1-mCitrine in that the strongest signal was in abaxial domains and in the stem (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine signal was uniformly detected throughout the root meristematic region and fainter signal detected in the root cap cells.
claims.source: TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine signal was uniformly detected throughout the root meristematic region and fainter signal detected in the root cap cells (Figure 5G, I–J and L; Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G, I-J, L and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: AFB1-mCitrine is very highly expressed throughout the root except for the columella, cortex, endodermis, and pericycle of the meristematic region.
claims.source: AFB1-mCitrine is very highly expressed throughout the root except for the columella, cortex, endodermis, and pericycle of the meristematic region (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: In embryos, TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine accumulate fairly uniformly throughout the embryos and suspensors.
claims.source: In embryos, TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine accumulate fairly uniformly throughout the embryos and suspensors while AFB4-mCitrine's signal was close to background levels and AFB1-mCitrine was undetectable (Figure 5T–Y).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5T-Y.

claims.claim: AFB4-mCitrine's signal in embryos was close to background levels.
claims.source: In embryos, TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine accumulate fairly uniformly throughout the embryos and suspensors while AFB4-mCitrine's signal was close to background levels and AFB1-mCitrine was undetectable (Figure 5T–Y).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5T-Y.

claims.claim: AFB1-mCitrine was undetectable in embryos.
claims.source: In embryos, TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine accumulate fairly uniformly throughout the embryos and suspensors while AFB4-mCitrine's signal was close to background levels and AFB1-mCitrine was undetectable (Figure 5T–Y).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5T-Y.

claims.claim: TIR1-mCitrine is primarily localized in nuclei.
claims.source: TIR1-mCitrine is primarily in nuclei while significant amounts of AFB2 through AFB5 are present in the cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 5S.

claims.claim: Significant amounts of AFB2 through AFB5 are present in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: TIR1-mCitrine is primarily in nuclei while significant amounts of AFB2 through AFB5 are present in the cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 5S.

claims.claim: AFB1-mCitrine appears primarily outside the nuclei.
claims.source: Strikingly, AFB1-mCitrine appears primarily outside the nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 5S.

claims.claim: TIR1 and AFB1 proteins exhibit contrasting patterns of primarily nuclear and cytoplasmic subcellular localizations, respectively.
claims.source: Hence, despite being from the same clade, TIR1 and AFB1 proteins exhibit contrasting patterns of primarily nuclear and cytoplasmic subcellular localizations, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the localization data.

claims.claim: Each of the TIR1/AFBs contributes to rapid root growth inhibition.
claims.source: The results in Figure 6 show that each of the TIR1/AFBs contributes to rapid root growth inhibition but that, surprisingly, the afb1-3 mutant is almost completely resistant to auxin indicating that AFB1 is the dominant auxin receptor for this response.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The afb1-3 mutant is almost completely resistant to auxin in the rapid root growth inhibition assay, indicating that AFB1 is the dominant auxin receptor for this response.
claims.source: The results in Figure 6 show that each of the TIR1/AFBs contributes to rapid root growth inhibition but that, surprisingly, the afb1-3 mutant is almost completely resistant to auxin indicating that AFB1 is the dominant auxin receptor for this response.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Expression of AFB1-mCitrine under control of the AFB1 promoter restored the wild-level of auxin response in the rapid root growth inhibition assay.
claims.source: Expression of AFB1-mCitrine under control of the AFB1 promoter restored the wild-level of auxin response.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The afb1 mutant is not affected in long-term inhibition of root growth.
claims.source: This includes long-term inhibition of root growth.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of rapid and long-term assays.

claims.claim: The afb1 mutant is a useful tool to discriminate between nongenomic and transcriptional auxin responses.
claims.source: Thus, the afb1 mutant is a useful tool to discriminate between nongenomic and transcriptional auxin responses.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the differential effects of afb1 on rapid vs. long-term responses.

claims.claim: The tir1afb1345 mutant exhibited a decrease in the gravitropic response during the initial lag phase compared to tir1afb345.
claims.source: Strikingly, the tir1afb1345 mutant exhibited an additional decrease in the gravitropic response during the initial lag phase demonstrating that AFB1 is required for this phase (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: AFB1 is required for the initial lag phase of gravitropic response.
claims.source: Strikingly, the tir1afb1345 mutant exhibited an additional decrease in the gravitropic response during the initial lag phase demonstrating that AFB1 is required for this phase (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The tir1afb1 line showed a similar decrease in the lag phase of gravitropism compared to tir1.
claims.source: The tir1afb1 line showed a similar decrease in the lag phase compared to tir1 (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: TIR1 also contributes to the early gravitropic response since the tir1afb1 double mutant showed a stronger delay compared to either single mutant.
claims.source: It seems likely that TIR1 also contributes to the early response since the tir1afb1 double mutant showed a stronger delay compared to either single mutant.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of gravitropism data.

claims.claim: Both afb1 AFB1-mCitrine lines responded appreciably faster than the afb1 mutant during the first 2 hr of gravitropic response.
claims.source: Further, both afb1 AFB1-mCitrine lines responded appreciably faster than the afb1 mutant during the first 2 hr with the brighter of the two mCitrine lines, line #7, exhibiting a difference by 30 min (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: AFB1 and the rapid response play a role at later stages of the gravitropic bending response.
claims.source: Interestingly, both mCitrine lines started to plateau earlier and at a reduced angle compared to wild type while afb1 plateaued later and at an increased angle, suggesting that AFB1 and the rapid response also play a role at later stages of the gravitropic bending response.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on gravitropism data.

claims.claim: For most auxin-regulated growth processes, the TIR/AFB proteins retain largely overlapping functions despite diverging approximately 400 MYA.
claims.source: Despite the fact that three major subclades were established approximately 400 MYA (Morris et al., 2018), our genetic studies reveal that for most auxin-regulated growth processes, the TIR/AFB proteins retain largely overlapping functions (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Morris et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 8.

claims.claim: TIR1 is most important for normal growth and development among the TIR1/AFB proteins.
claims.source: In general, TIR1 is most important for normal growth and development, but AFB5 and AFB2, and to a lesser extent AFB3 and AFB4, also play significant roles.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the genetic analysis.

claims.claim: TIR1 has a major role in the root while AFB5 is relatively more important in hypocotyl and inflorescence development.
claims.source: Spatial differences are also apparent; TIR1 has a major role in the root while AFB5 is relatively more important in hypocotyl and inflorescence development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on phenotypic analysis.

claims.claim: The relative importance of individual TIR1/AFB proteins in various organs are at least partly related to differences in expression.
claims.source: Although all six genes are broadly expressed, it appears that the relative importance of individual TIR1/AFB proteins in various organs are at least partly related to differences in expression.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on expression pattern analysis.

claims.claim: AFB5 is more broadly expressed than the other genes in the inflorescence.
claims.source: For example, AFB5 is more broadly expressed than the other genes in the inflorescence while in the root, TIR1 and AFB2 are most highly expressed.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on fluorescence imaging.

claims.claim: In the root, TIR1 and AFB2 are most highly expressed.
claims.source: For example, AFB5 is more broadly expressed than the other genes in the inflorescence while in the root, TIR1 and AFB2 are most highly expressed.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on fluorescence imaging.

claims.claim: The AFB4 gene is expressed at a lower level in all tissues consistent with its relatively minor role.
claims.source: The AFB4 gene is expressed at a lower level in all tissues consistent with its relatively minor role.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on fluorescence imaging and phenotypic analysis.

claims.claim: The levels of the TIR1/AFB proteins are not uniform throughout the plant.
claims.source: Our studies demonstrate that the levels of the TIR1/AFB proteins are not uniform throughout the plant.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on fluorescence imaging.

claims.claim: TIR1/AFB levels can be dynamic in a changing environment.
claims.source: Earlier experiments also showed that TIR1/AFB levels can be dynamic in a changing environment (Vidal et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Vidal et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2016.

claims.claim: There is an asymmetric distribution of TIR1-mCitrine across flower primordia.
claims.source: Given the debate over an auxin-response asymmetry across shoot organ primordia (Bhatia et al., 2019; Guan et al., 2019), it is particularly interesting that we see an asymmetric distribution of TIR1-mCitrine across flower primordia.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis reveals that the TIR1/AFB auxin receptor family in Arabidopsis represents three of four ancient clades established over 400 million years ago, with gene duplications coinciding with whole genome duplication events. AFB1 has accumulated significantly more non-synonymous changes than TIR1 and contains F-box substitutions that weaken CUL1 interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C13, C117-C121 collectively provide strong phylogenetic evidence supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and appropriate citations. The evolutionary timeline, gene duplication events, and AFB1's unique evolutionary trajectory are well-documented through branch length analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction.

results.result: Loss of all six TIR1/AFB proteins causes fully penetrant embryo lethality with defects beginning at the 2-cell stage, including abnormal cell division orientations, delayed and symmetrical hypophysis division, suspensor proliferation, and eventual seed abortion.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C28-C35 are strongly supported by detailed embryo imaging in Figure 3 with quantitative measurements of division angles and specific cell counts. The progression of defects from early embryogenesis through abortion is well-documented, establishing the essential role of TIR1/AFB proteins in embryo development.

results.result: A single wild-type allele of either TIR1 or AFB2 is sufficient to support plant viability throughout development, though these plants are severely compromised and rarely produce seeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C17-C18 are directly demonstrated by the viability of tir1/+ afb12345 and afb2/+ tir1afb1345 plants shown in Figure 1B. This remarkable finding demonstrates extreme functional redundancy, though the severe phenotypes and near-sterility indicate these single alleles provide minimal function.

results.result: Comprehensive genetic analysis of all 63 mutant combinations reveals extensive functional overlap among TIR1/AFB proteins except AFB1, with TIR1 being most important overall, AFB5 critical for inflorescence development, and AFB1 having minimal effects on most processes but suppressing lateral root formation in certain genetic backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C15-C16, C20-C25, C68, C70-C71, C83 are supported by systematic phenotypic analysis across all mutant combinations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 2, Supplementary file 1). The quantitative measurements of multiple phenotypes with appropriate statistical analysis provide strong evidence for the functional relationships, though the lateral root suppression by AFB1 (C22-C23) is somewhat unexpected and mechanistically unclear.

results.result: In tir1afb235 quadruple mutant embryos, auxin-responsive markers (DR5, WOX5) are absent, PIN1 expression is reduced and mislocalized, PIN7 is ectopically expressed in the embryo proper, and NTT is progressively lost from suspensor cells, indicating severe disruption of auxin signaling and patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40, C88, C91 are well-supported by confocal imaging in Figure 4 with specific cell counts for each marker. The complete absence of DR5 and WOX5 signals (0/10 and 0/11 mutants vs. 26/26 and 28/28 siblings) provides strong quantitative evidence, though the biological interpretation of ectopic PIN7 expression (C38) remains speculative.

results.result: AFB1 is the dominant receptor for rapid auxin-dependent inhibition of root growth, with the afb1 mutant being almost completely resistant to auxin in this response while remaining sensitive to long-term root growth inhibition, providing a tool to discriminate genomic from non-genomic auxin responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C57-C61, C109 are strongly supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 6 showing afb1's near-complete resistance to 10 nM IAA in the rapid response (20 min) while maintaining sensitivity in long-term assays. The complementation with AFB1-mCitrine (C59) confirms specificity. This is a major discovery revealing functional specialization.

results.result: AFB1 exhibits primarily cytoplasmic localization in contrast to TIR1's nuclear localization, with AFB2-AFB5 showing intermediate distributions. This differential localization may explain AFB1's specialized role in rapid auxin responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C53-C56, C100, C105-C106, C110 are supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements in Figure 5S showing clear differences in nuclear vs. cytoplasmic distribution. However, the causal link between cytoplasmic localization and rapid response function (C6, C110) remains correlative rather than mechanistic, representing reasonable speculation rather than demonstrated causation.

results.result: AFB1 is required for the initial lag phase of gravitropic response, with tir1afb1345 showing decreased early gravitropic bending compared to tir1afb345. Both TIR1 and AFB1 contribute to this early response, and AFB1 may also affect later stages of gravitropic bending.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67, C112-C113 are supported by gravitropism time-course data in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The differential effects during the lag phase are clearly demonstrated, though the contribution of TIR1 (C65) is stated as 'likely' based on additive effects in the double mutant, and the role in later stages (C67) is more speculative.

results.result: TIR1/AFB proteins show distinct spatial expression patterns: AFB5 is broadly expressed in inflorescences, TIR1/AFB2/AFB3 are restricted to young primordia and meristems, AFB1 shows complementary expression in abaxial domains, AFB4 is barely detectable, and AFB1 is undetectable in embryos. These expression differences partially explain functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C52, C72-C76, C102 are well-supported by comprehensive fluorescence imaging in Figure 5 across multiple tissues. The expression patterns are clearly documented, though the causal relationship between expression patterns and functional importance (C72) is correlative. AFB4's low expression (C46, C51, C75) is consistent with its minor functional role.

results.result: The penetrance of the rootless seedling phenotype in tir1afb23, tir1afb123, and tir1afb245 lines is temperature-sensitive, being significantly lower at 20°C than at 17°C or 23°C, suggesting temperature sensitivity of the auxin regulatory system.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D with appropriate statistical testing (Fisher's exact test). The temperature-dependent penetrance is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanistic interpretation (C27) that 'aspects of the auxin regulatory system are sensitive to temperature' is a reasonable but general inference.

results.result: The tir1-1 allele does not act as a dominant-negative, as heterozygotes for tir1-1, tir1-10, and tir1-9 show similar semi-dominant phenotypes, and tir1-9 and tir1-10 produce no detectable transcript.
results.evaluation: Claim C14 is supported by root elongation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B comparing heterozygotes for three alleles, with appropriate citations. The logic is sound: if tir1-1 were dominant-negative, it should show a stronger phenotype than null alleles, which it does not. This resolves a controversy in the literature.

results.result: Gametophytically-expressed TIR1/AFBs do not contribute to gametophytic viability, as the sextuple mutant is transmitted at near-Mendelian ratios through both pollen (49.4%) and female gametophyte (47.9%).
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C95 are supported by transmission rate data in Supplementary file 2 with appropriate statistical tests (χ² test, p=0.81 and 0.43). The near-50% transmission rates provide strong evidence against a gametophytic requirement, though the authors appropriately note caveats about perdurance and minor roles that cannot be ruled out.

results.result: 32% of tir1afb1245 siliques have only one valve instead of the normal two valves.
results.evaluation: Claim C19 is directly supported by the observation and quantification shown in Figure 1C. This is a clear morphological phenotype, though it represents a descriptive observation rather than a mechanistic finding.

results.result: TIR1/AFB protein levels are dynamic and can be regulated by environmental signals through miR393, which targets TIR1, AFB2, and AFB3 to modulate lateral root formation and hypocotyl elongation. An asymmetric distribution of TIR1-mCitrine is observed across flower primordia.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 are supported by appropriate citations (Vidal et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016; Jones-Rhoades and Bartel, 2004; Navarro et al., 2006; Pucciariello et al., 2018) and imaging data. However, these are primarily literature-based claims with the asymmetric TIR1 distribution (C78) being a new observation that relates to ongoing debates in the field.

results.result: Previous in vitro and yeast-based studies have documented biochemical differences among TIR1/AFB family members.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are literature-based with appropriate citations (Calderón Villalobos et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2017). These provide context for the current work but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: The retention of overlapping functions among TIR1/AFB paralogs may reflect stricter constraints on protein function, or the paralogs may contribute to robustness of the auxin signaling system.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are explicitly speculative ('It is possible that...', 'One possibility is that...') and represent hypotheses rather than tested conclusions. While these are reasonable interpretations of the extensive functional overlap observed, they lack direct experimental support and remain uncertain.

results.result: The importance of auxin in embryo patterning is well-established, with auxin signaling first apparent in the apical cell. Similar embryo defects are observed in other auxin mutants affecting response, synthesis, and transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87, C89 are literature-based with extensive citations (Palovaara et al., 2016; Friml et al., 2003; Berleth and Jürgens, 1993; and others). These provide important context for interpreting the TIR1/AFB mutant phenotypes but represent established knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: None of the other auxin mutants exhibit the fully penetrant embryo-lethal phenotype observed for the tir1afb235 quadruple and tir1afb12345 sextuple mutants.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 is supported by comparison with literature on other auxin mutants. This distinguishes the TIR1/AFB receptor mutants from other components of auxin signaling, synthesis, and transport, highlighting the unique severity of complete receptor loss.

results.result: Proliferation of suspensor cells in tir1afb235 mutants is associated with reduced PIN7-Venus and NTT-YPet expression, suggesting the TIR1/AFB pathway maintains suspensor cell fate. Ectopic PIN7 expression in the embryo proper may indicate normally repressed expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by marker expression data in Figure 4 with citation to Rademacher et al., 2012. However, the mechanistic interpretation about maintaining suspensor fate is inferential, and the speculation about PIN7 repression (C94) is explicitly uncertain ('The reason for this is unclear but...').

results.result: It is possible that auxin acts in gametophytes through a non-canonical pathway such as auxin binding to ETTIN protein.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is explicitly speculative ('it is possible that...') with a citation to Simonini et al., 2016. This represents an alternative hypothesis to explain potential auxin function in gametophytes despite lack of TIR1/AFB requirement, but lacks direct experimental support.

results.result: AFB1 has undergone pronounced functional changes during Brassicales diversification, can interact with Aux/IAA proteins but assembles into SCF complexes less efficiently than other TIR1/AFBs, with F-box substitutions appearing 45-65 million years ago.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99, C101 are supported by phylogenetic data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), citations (Edger et al., 2018; Dharmasiri et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2015), and localization data (Figure 5). The evolutionary timeline and biochemical properties are well-documented, though the functional consequences are partially inferred.

results.result: AFB1 appears to have a negative effect on lateral root initiation in afb234 and afb345 lines despite not being expressed in the pericycle, suggesting a non-cell-autonomous effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by genetic data showing suppression of lateral root phenotypes (C23). However, the non-cell-autonomous interpretation (C104) is speculative based on expression patterns and lacks direct mechanistic evidence. results.result: Auxin treatment causes rapid responses in Arabidopsis roots including increased cytosolic Ca++, apoplast alkalinization, and root growth inhibition. Recent studies show that rapid root growth inhibition and root hair membrane depolarization require TIR1/AFBs.
